arguments.content:
---
name: beautiful-frontend
description: This skill guides the creation or substantial visual revision of browser-rendered interfaces—marketing pages, product surfaces, dashboards, commerce, editorial experiences, prototypes, and extensions to existing sites—when the task requires layout, styling, interaction, or art-direction decisions. It should not be loaded for backend-only work, non-visual refactors, isolated logic fixes, CLI or native-app work, copy-only tasks, or tiny UI corrections whose appearance is already fully specified.
---

# Build a Designed Interface

## Establish the design logic before coding

- Read the brief, repository, existing screens, and bundled assets first; treat existing product conventions as constraints, not debris to replace.
- Write a private one-sentence design thesis: “This should feel ___ because ___; the user should notice ___ first.” Every major visual choice must support it.
- Choose three specific tonal words with visual consequences (for example “archival, exacting, warm,” not “modern, clean, beautiful”). Map each to a choice in type, spacing, color, or motion.
- Identify the primary user action and the one piece of evidence that makes it credible. Give each a distinct visual role above the fold.
- Pick one subject-derived motif—such as ledger rules, crop marks, contour lines, ticket perforations, stacked specimens, or a timeline—and repeat it in only 2–3 places. Do not add decoration unrelated to the subject.
- Decide the density from the job: sparse for persuasion or luxury, moderate for general products, compact for monitoring and repeated operations. Do not use landing-page spacing in a dashboard.
- If extending an existing interface, preserve its type scale, spacing rhythm, component grammar, and interaction patterns; create distinction through composition and content, not a competing design system.

## Build hierarchy from content

- Put the most specific, differentiating claim in the largest type; never make a generic category label the visual headline.
- Make the first viewport answer, in order: what this is, why it matters, what to do next, and why to trust it.
- Give each section one job. Remove any section whose message duplicates another, and merge fragments that cannot support their own composition.
- Use real task-relevant labels and plausible data. Avoid “Lorem ipsum,” “Feature 1,” fabricated testimonials, and ornamental metrics.
- Keep eyebrow labels to 2–5 words, headlines to roughly 8–12 words, prose to 45–75 characters per line, and primary button labels to a verb plus object.
- Establish three levels of emphasis per region: primary, supporting, quiet. If everything has a border, color, or bold weight, hierarchy has failed.

## Choose a visual system, not familiar defaults

- Inspect available fonts before choosing any. Prefer a distinctive bundled face for display and a highly readable face for body; use at most two families and three weights total.
- Do not introduce Inter, Arial, Roboto, or a generic system stack as an aesthetic shortcut. Use system type only when speed, neutrality, or native-product continuity is part of the thesis.
- Set a deliberate responsive scale with `clamp()`: body 15–18px, supporting text 12–14px, display text about 40–76px on desktop and 32–48px on mobile.
- Tighten display tracking slightly and use 0.95–1.08 line-height; keep body tracking normal and line-height at 1.45–1.7. Never center long body copy.
- Derive spacing from one base unit, usually 4px or 5px. Use a restrained sequence such as 4/8/12/20/32/52/84 rather than arbitrary gaps.
- Select one dominant neutral family, one functional accent, and at most one supporting hue. Assign colors semantic roles before applying them.
- Avoid the generated-UI palette: purple-to-blue gradients, glowing cyan on navy, and evenly distributed pastel blobs unless the subject explicitly calls for them.
- If using a gradient, keep it within neighboring hues or use it as subtle light falloff; it must explain depth, focus, or brand—not merely fill space.
- Make surfaces legible through tone first. Reserve shadows for true elevation; use borders, inset rules, or small tone shifts for grouping.
- Use one corner-radius family: sharp 0–4px, tailored 6–10px, or soft 12–20px. Pills are only for tags, statuses, filters, or capsule controls—not every container.

## Compose the page

- Use a grid, but break symmetry intentionally once per major view: an offset headline, oversized visual, narrow evidence rail, or controlled overlap.
- Align unrelated sections to shared anchors. A page looks designed when text, imagery, controls, and rules repeatedly begin or end on the same lines.
- Alternate section rhythm rather than stacking identical centered bands. Vary at least two of: column ratio, density, alignment, background treatment, or media placement.
- Do not wrap every idea in a card. Use whitespace for separation, rules for sequence, bands for category changes, and cards only for independently actionable or comparable units.
- Avoid the default hero formula of centered headline, two buttons, and a floating rounded dashboard. Choose a composition justified by the content: editorial split, product-in-context, evidence-first, annotated object, or dense operational overview.
- Let one element dominate each viewport. Supporting objects should be visibly quieter by scale, contrast, or position.
- Use overlap only where it conveys layering or relationship, and ensure the overlapped objects remain intelligible at all breakpoints.
- Keep desktop content width deliberate: roughly 1120–1320px for rich layouts, 680–760px for reading, with side gutters of at least 24px.

## Make imagery and detail earn their place

- Prefer provided product imagery, diagrams, or content artifacts over stock decoration. Crop around the subject, not merely to fit a rectangle.
- Do not fake a product screenshot with vague boxes if a credible interface can be built; show enough concrete labels, states, and data to withstand a second glance.
- When no imagery exists, create a subject-specific composition from type, rules, data, or simple geometry rather than a generic abstract orb.
- Use one icon style and consistent optical size. Do not use emoji as interface icons; do not mix outlined, filled, and hand-drawn symbols without semantic reason.
- Pair icons with labels for unfamiliar actions. Keep icon-only controls for universal actions and give them accessible names and tooltips where appropriate.
- Add a few high-value details: a precise selected state, useful empty state, contextual annotation, unit label, data timestamp, or progress indication. Do not scatter decorative microcopy.
- Make charts communicate a comparison or trend. Label important values directly, mute scaffolding, and never add a chart solely to make a dashboard look busy.

## Design interaction as states

- Implement hover, focus-visible, active, disabled, loading, empty, error, and success states for controls that can reach them.
- Make the entire apparent hit target interactive. Interactive targets should be at least 44×44px on touch layouts, with no hover-only essential information.
- Use motion to explain entry, hierarchy, or state change: 140–220ms for controls and 300–600ms for composed transitions, usually with deceleration on entry and acceleration on exit.
- Animate transform and opacity when possible. Avoid layout-thrashing transitions, continuous floating, cursor-following effects, and unrelated elements arriving from every direction.
- Limit initial-load choreography to one sequence with 30–80ms staggering and no more than 6 animated groups. Disable nonessential motion under `prefers-reduced-motion`.
- Keep navigation and primary actions predictable even when the visual treatment is expressive.

## Make responsiveness a recomposition

- Design and verify at 360px, 768px, and 1440px; add breakpoints where content fails, not because a framework names them.
- On small screens, preserve hierarchy by changing composition: stack, reorder, crop, collapse, or turn comparison tables into labeled rows. Do not merely shrink everything.
- Keep mobile gutters at 16–24px, prevent orphaned single-word headline lines when feasible, and remove decorative overlaps that obscure content.
- Do not hide core content on mobile. Replace secondary navigation and dense utilities with an explicit accessible disclosure pattern.
- Constrain media with aspect ratios and `object-fit`; reserve space before load so layout does not jump.

## Accessibility is part of the visual specification

- Use semantic landmarks and heading order; use buttons for actions and links for navigation rather than styled generic containers.
- Meet at least 4.5:1 contrast for normal text and 3:1 for large text and essential UI boundaries; never encode status by hue alone.
- Provide a clearly visible `:focus-visible` treatment that works on every surface, typically a 2–3px ring with offset.
- Give form controls persistent labels, concise error text adjacent to the field, and instructions before the user encounters the constraint.
- Preserve zoom, keyboard operation, logical tab order, and readable content when text expands; never disable outlines without a replacement.

## Implementation discipline

- Reuse the project’s framework, tokens, components, and icon library before adding alternatives. Do not add a dependency for a detail achievable with existing code or CSS.
- Define repeated color, spacing, radius, and typography values as tokens; keep exceptional values local and intentional.
- Build the semantic structure and responsive geometry first, then typography and color, then states and motion. Decoration cannot rescue weak hierarchy.
- Keep decorative layers non-interactive and out of the accessibility tree. Ensure pseudo-elements and absolute positioning cannot intercept clicks.
- Preserve functional requirements while editing visuals; do not replace working interactions with static mockups.

## Reject these failure modes before finishing

- Remove any section that resembles a reusable template more than the product: generic icon grids, stat strips without context, endless rounded cards, logo clouds made from text, or gratuitous testimonial carousels.
- Remove at least one unnecessary container, border, badge, or decorative effect from each visually crowded region.
- Check for repeated sentence lengths, identical section silhouettes, uniform spacing, and equal emphasis; introduce contrast where monotony is accidental.
